title: The Promises and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence for Teachers: a Systematic Review of Research
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how artificial intelligence has been used in relation to teachers, focusing on what AI offers teachers, what challenges teachers face when using AI, what kinds of teacher data have been used in AI research, and what roles teachers play in developing AI-based educational systems. The authors note that AI in education has often been discussed in terms of student learning or technical development, while the teacher perspective has been comparatively neglected. To address this gap, they conducted a systematic review of empirical studies on teachers’ use of AI applications and machine-learning methods in educational settings.

The review synthesized 44 English-language empirical studies from the Web of Science database published over roughly the previous 20 years up to September 14, 2020. Included studies concerned pre-service or in-service teachers, AI applications for teaching, or AI/machine-learning analyses of teacher-related data. Across these studies, teachers were involved in several ways: as sources of training data for AI systems, as providers of student information, as graders validating automated scoring systems, and as users of AI-supported tools for planning, instruction, and assessment. The review found that common teacher data types included self-reports, grading data, observations, interviews, and video, with relatively little use of multimodal physiological data.

The population and context covered by the reviewed studies were broad rather than tied to one intervention or one site. The review focused primarily on K-12 contexts and teacher-related educational settings, including elementary, middle, high school, and mixed or unspecified K-12 environments. Subject domains represented in the reviewed literature included English, literacy, mathematics, science, ICT, early childhood, and mixed domains. The paper itself did not test a direct intervention; instead, it aggregated evidence across studies of AI-supported planning tools, monitoring systems, automated scoring, adaptive feedback systems, and predictive models related to teachers and classrooms.

The main conclusions are that AI shows promise for supporting teachers in planning, implementation, and assessment—for example by helping identify student needs, monitor classroom processes in real time, reduce workload, provide immediate feedback, and support automated assessment. At the same time, the review identifies important challenges, including limited reliability and technical capacity of current AI systems, context dependence, insufficient school infrastructure, and limited teacher technological knowledge. The authors conclude that teachers remain central to AI-enabled education and should be more deeply involved in AI design and development. They also call for more research on pre-service teacher education and more sophisticated, multimodal, pedagogically grounded AI systems.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review, but it is not a meta-analysis and does not provide pooled causal estimates on direct K-12 student literacy outcomes. The evidence synthesized is largely descriptive and heterogeneous, with many included studies focused on teacher use, tool development, prediction, or assessment rather than strong comparative impact designs.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful benefits for teacher productivity and implementation support, but impact is indirect and unclear for student literacy outcomes, with no pooled effect sizes. Because this is not a direct comparative student-outcome study and findings are mixed at the systems level, overall impact is best classified as unclear.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of AI applications used by teachers or built from teacher data in K-12 education, including automated essay scoring, intelligent/adaptive supports, monitoring tools, and predictive models; the paper does not evaluate a single student-facing intervention directly.

finding.finding_summary: Across the 44 empirical studies synthesized, the review reports that AI was commonly described as helping teachers reduce workload, automate assessment, monitor students in real time, and support timely intervention. These are narrative synthesis findings from included studies rather than pooled effect estimates; no meta-analytic effect size, confidence interval, or standardized variance statistics were reported.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of teacher-reported and study-reported advantages such as workload reduction, timely monitoring, immediate feedback, automated scoring, and planning support
finding.study_size: 44 studies in the review; underlying participant counts vary by included study

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that research on teachers' AI use has increased, especially after 2017, and identifies institutional promises for planning, implementation, and assessment, alongside barriers such as limited reliability of algorithms, weak technical infrastructure, teacher knowledge gaps, and poor transfer across contexts. These conclusions are based on qualitative aggregation of the 44 included studies and do not include pooled causal estimates.
finding.measure: Systematic review coding of publication trends, teacher roles in AI development, reported implementation challenges, and implications for school adoption
